# How to build a simple study schedule in the weeks before a big exam

> **In short:** The schedule that works is one that fits your real life: count back from the exam, rank topics by weight and weakness, place hard work in your strongest hours, and bake in breaks and a weekly self-check.

That big exam is three weeks out and the textbook feels taller than your motivation. A schedule won't learn the material for you, but it will give you a clear next step every morning. Here's how to build one in five concrete steps, no fancy app required.

## Before you start
- **The exam date and a list of what it covers** — a syllabus (the official list of topics the test will cover), a course outline, or your own chapter list. Anything works.
- **A calendar you can scribble on** — paper, a notes app, a spreadsheet, or a printed weekly view. Whatever you'll actually look at.
- **Roughly 45 minutes** for the first pass, then about 10 minutes a week to adjust it.
- **Optional:** an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or any other) that you can paste a topic into and ask "break this into five subtopics in order of difficulty". Helpful, not required.

## Step 1 — Count back from the exam and map your weeks

Open your calendar and put a big mark on the test day. Then count backwards in weeks and give each block a short label: "W1 — foundation", "W2 — depth", "W3 — review & mock". If you have one week, one block is fine; if you have six, mark the first as warm-up and the last as buffer.

What you'll see on screen (or on paper): a blank week-by-week grid with the exam on the right edge and today on the left. Each week now carries a short phrase naming what kind of work belongs there.

What happens next: the mountain stops being one giant pile. You're not staring at "everything I don't know" anymore — you're staring at "what I should do this week". That shift matters more than the exact labels.

If it looks different on your device: a paper planner works exactly the same way. If you'd rather skip the labels, just write the week numbers above each column.

💬 Example: For a 21-day window, write `W1 — foundation | W2 — depth | W3 — review & mock`. For 10 days, write `W1 — learn + drill | W2 — review + mock`.

You'll know it worked when you can point at any week and say, in one short phrase, what it's for.

## Step 2 — List every topic, then rank by weight and weakness

Grab your syllabus and turn each chapter, lecture, or module into a single line on a list. Then walk down the list twice. First pass — weight: how much of the exam is this topic worth? Second pass — weakness: how shaky do you feel about it right now? Mark each item H, M, or L for both. Anything that scores H on either list goes into your "must-cover" pile.

What you'll see on screen: a plain list of maybe 15–30 lines, each with two short codes beside it. Some items glow — H on weight, H on weakness, or both.

What happens next: your priorities stop being a guess. You study what matters and where you actually need help, instead of the chapter that's loudest in your textbook.

If it looks different on your device: if you don't have a syllabus, use the table of contents of your main textbook as a stand-in. Don't have time to rank every item? Pick the five topics that feel heaviest and rank only those.

💬 Example: `Ch 4 — Cell biology | weight: H | weakness: H`, `Ch 7 — Statistics | weight: M | weakness: L`, `Ch 11 — Lab safety | weight: L | weakness: M`.

You'll know it worked when you can name your top three must-cover topics without looking at the list.

## Step 3 — Block daily sessions around your real peak energy

Look at your real day — classes, work, commute, sleep, meals, kids, the dog. Find the 60–90 minute window when your brain is sharpest. For many people that's morning, but yours might be late evening. Carve that window out, on as many days as you can, and assign it your highest-priority topic from Step 2. Lower-priority or easier review work fills the smaller, lower-energy pockets.

What you'll see on screen: your week, with one or two solid blocks per day labeled with a topic from your list, and the rest of the day left alone. You're not scheduling every minute — you're protecting the minutes that matter.

What happens next: study time stops fighting the rest of your life. You stop promising "8pm study" when you know 8pm-you is half-asleep, and start promising "7am study" because you've seen the pattern before.

If it looks different on your device: if your week is wildly uneven (one day free, four days slammed), put your longest block on the free day and let the slammed days carry shorter 20–30 minute reviews. That's still a schedule.

💬 Example: a week might look like `Mon 7–8am: Ch 4 cell biology | Mon 8:30–9pm: 30 min flashcards Ch 7 | Tue 7–8am: Ch 4 problems | Wed 6:30–7:30pm: Ch 5`.

You'll know it worked when you can glance at any weekday and see exactly which topic you're doing and when.

## Step 4 — Bake in breaks, reviews and a weekly self-check

A schedule without breaks collapses by Wednesday. Inside each daily block, add a 5–10 minute break at the halfway mark — walk, water, stare out the window. Add one short review slot near the end of each week where you re-read notes from earlier weeks for 30 minutes. And add a 15-minute Sunday-or-Monday self-check: what got done, what didn't, what needs to move.

What you'll see on screen: your week now has a little padding. Each big block carries a small break in it, and the week ends with a small review window instead of another cram.

What happens next: you stop "forgetting" week-one material by week three, because you actually see it again. And when life knocks out a block, your self-check catches it on Monday before it becomes a crisis.

If it looks different on your device: if you study on an app rather than paper, look for a "split session" or "add break" toggle — most study apps have one. If your week has no good review slot, fold a 10-minute review into the last few minutes of two of your regular blocks.

💬 Example: in your daily block, write `7:00–7:45 work | 7:45–7:55 break | 7:55–8:30 work`. For the weekly self-check, write a single line: `Sun 6pm — what got done / what didn't / what moves`.

You'll know it worked when you can list, without looking, what you reviewed last week.

## Step 5 — Test the plan with one real practice question

Before you commit, run the schedule once. Pick the highest-priority topic from Step 2 and do a single timed practice question on it — past paper, end-of-chapter problem, flashcard. Don't grade yourself harshly; just notice whether the time you scheduled was actually enough. If the question felt impossible in that window, the schedule needs more space for that topic. If it felt comfortable, the schedule is roughly right.

What you'll see on screen (or on paper): one practice question, a timer, your honest answer, and a one-sentence note to yourself about whether the time was enough.

What happens next: you have real feedback instead of a guess. The schedule becomes a working draft instead of a wish list, and you can adjust it during Sunday's self-check instead of on exam eve.

If it looks different on your device: no practice questions handy? Try explaining the topic out loud for two minutes, as if teaching a friend. If you can't, the schedule needs more time on that topic. Same signal, different test.

💬 Example: set a 10-minute timer, answer one past-paper question on your H-weighted, H-weakness topic, then write one sentence: `Felt too short — add 20 min next week` or `Felt OK — keep as is`.

You'll know it worked when you can point to one concrete signal that says whether your plan is realistic or not.

## Common mistakes
- **Scheduling every minute of every day.** The plan dies by day 3 because real life interrupts. Protect your peak-energy window; leave the rest of the day alone.
- **Studying your favorite topics first.** Comfort is not a priority. Follow the H/H ranking from Step 2; save easy wins for low-energy pockets.
- **Skipping the weekly self-check.** If you never look back, you'll keep repeating the same missed blocks. A 10-minute Sunday review catches drift before it becomes a disaster.

## What this means for you
- **If you're a student:** A schedule like this fits on a single page, which means you'll actually look at it. It also makes saying "no" to extra plans easier — your peak block is non-negotiable.
- **If you're an adult returning to study:** Your "real life" has more moving parts than a college student's. Use the energy-honest version from Step 3: protect one good block, fill the edges, and don't pretend you have four free hours if you don't.
- **If you're helping a teen or younger student:** Sit with them through Steps 1–2 and let them run Steps 3–5 themselves. The schedule works best when it's theirs.

## Try it now
Open your calendar app or a piece of paper. Mark the exam date, count backwards, and write down the five topics that scare you most. That's the whole first pass — about five minutes. Everything else builds from there.
